findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator applies math.floor/ceil to a datetime key and raises TypeError
findings.body: OptimizedCursorPaginator inherits BasePaginator's cursor machinery but overrides get_item_key with math.floor/math.ceil on getattr(item, self.key). The endpoint uses order_by="-datetime", so self.key is "datetime" and the value is a datetime object, which math.floor rejects with TypeError. build_cursor calls key(results[0]) whenever the first page has results, so every request with optimized_pagination=true from an admin that returns at least one audit log row fails with a 500. Unlike DateTimePaginator, this class also lacks the strftime-to-milliseconds conversion, and value_from_cursor returns the raw integer, so cursors could not be used for datetime comparisons even if the TypeError were avoided. The new code path cannot work for its only intended use.

findings.title: Negative-offset branch always fails inside Django slicing and is reachable from user input
findings.body: The 'advanced' branch passes a negative cursor.offset directly into queryset[start_offset:stop]. Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ rejects negative indices with ValueError('Negative indexing is not supported.'), so this branch never returns data. The offset comes from Cursor.from_string, which accepts any integer from the request's cursor parameter (cursors.py line 59). An admin who sends an opted-in request with a cursor such as 0:-1:0 gets a 500 instead of a 400. The comment says the branch gives access to data beyond normal bounds, which it does not do. Negative offsets are never validated, so the branch is dead code that also turns malformed input into a server error.

findings.title: Base paginator silently clamps negative next-cursor offsets for all paginators
findings.body: BasePaginator.get_result now uses start_offset = max(0, offset) for next cursors but leaves prev cursors unclamped. This shared base class is used by DateTimePaginator, which the audit log endpoint uses on every default request, so the change alters behavior well beyond the opt-in path. A forged next cursor with a negative offset is now silently served from the start of the result set instead of failing, while a forged prev cursor with a negative offset still raises from Django slicing. Invalid input is now accepted inconsistently. The inline comment that this is 'safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions' is wrong: the queryset rejects negative slices, and the clamp is what changes the outcome. The existing code validates offsets elsewhere (for example the `if self.offset < 0` checks in other paginators), so this should be an explicit validation or be reverted.

findings.title: enable_advanced dereferences organization_context.member, which may be None, on every request
findings.body: enable_advanced is evaluated unconditionally, not only when optimized_pagination=true. RpcUserOrganizationContext.member is optional. For a caller that is not a superuser and has no organization membership record (for example a non-member who passes OrganizationAuditPermission through another grant), `organization_context.member.has_global_access` raises AttributeError, so the whole endpoint returns a 500, including the default pagination path that previously worked. Guard the access with `organization_context.member is not None`, or evaluate the flag only when use_optimized is true.

findings.title: Comment claims permissions are enforced at the queryset level, which this branch does not do
findings.body: The comment says 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level'. Nothing in this branch checks permissions. The endpoint's permission class has already run, and the queryset is only filtered by organization_id. The comment justifies a deliberately wider access path, which would mislead future maintainers into treating unchecked negative-offset access as vetted. The claim should be removed, and the branch should be removed unless a real use case is demonstrated.

findings.title: The 'optimized' path issues the same query as the default path, so it gives no performance benefit
findings.body: The opted-in branch uses the same queryset, ordering, and slicing as DateTimePaginator. The only differences are the broken get_item_key and the unreachable negative-offset branch. The PR title and comments claim high-performance, efficient traversal, but no query, index, or benchmark change supports that. The PR description is just 'Test 1', so there is no stated rationale or measurement. The comments and title should not claim a performance gain unless one is demonstrated.

findings.title: Comment says negative cursor offsets are supported, but nothing validates or handles them
findings.body: The added comments state that negative offsets are allowed and 'enable efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions'. The change here is only a comment, and Cursor accepts whatever int() returns, including values parsed from untrusted request input via from_string. The paginators either raise on negative slices or silently clamp them, so the comment describes behavior that does not exist and documents an input the server never validates. Remove the comment or add real validation.

findings.title: New paginator, new query parameter, and changed base behavior have no tests
findings.body: The PR adds a public experimental query parameter (optimized_pagination), a new OptimizedCursorPaginator class with its own get_result and get_item_key, and changes BasePaginator.get_result, which every DateTimePaginator caller relies on. No tests are added or updated. A single request from an admin with at least one audit log row would have exposed the TypeError in get_item_key. Tests should cover: the opted-in admin path with rows, the non-admin fallback to DateTimePaginator, the member-less caller case, and how negative cursor offsets are handled on both the next and prev paths.
